explainers.title: Hello and welcome to Collaboration
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome to Unit 5 of Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. So far, most of your work in this subject has been about your own thinking: what you find out, and what you notice. This unit is different, because it is all about working with other people. The skill is called Collaboration, and it is one of the most useful skills you will ever learn.

Here are all six thinking skills of Global Perspectives, so you can see where this unit fits:

This whole unit is about the fifth skill: Collaboration. Almost nothing big in the world is made by one person alone. A school is run by a team of teachers. A clinic is staffed by a team of nurses and doctors. A family meal is cooked and shared by several hands. Herders in the countryside around Hargeisa move their animals together, watching out for one another. When you learn to collaborate well, you can help build things that would be far too big to build on your own.

A learner who practises collaboration now will be a better teammate, friend and neighbour for their whole life. That is why we teach it on purpose, not just hope it happens by accident.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful, tidy way.
Analysis — breaking a topic into parts and asking why things happen.
Evaluation — deciding how strong an idea or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn and how you change your mind.
Collaboration — working well together with other people to reach a shared goal.
Communication — sharing your ideas clearly so that others understand you.

explainers.title: So what is collaboration?
explainers.body:
Here is a simple meaning you can keep: collaboration means working together with other people to reach a shared goal. That goal has a special name in this unit. We call it a shared outcome: the one result the whole team is working towards.

Good collaboration is really three things joined together, and this unit will teach all three:

Notice that collaboration is not just sitting in the same room as other people. Five children doing their own separate thing at the same table are not collaborating. A team is collaborating when they share one outcome, share out the work, and help each other reach it. That is the skill you will build.
bullets: Sharing ideas — offering your own ideas, and listening carefully to everyone else's.
Planning together — deciding who does what, and how long each job will take.
Solving problems together — finding fair answers to problems and disagreements when they come up.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You might wonder how you can learn teamwork when you study mostly at your own pace, on your own. That is a very good question, and the answer is the heart of this unit. You will plan and practise on your own with your AI tutor, then do the real teamwork with your group in your teacher sessions.

So the pattern all the way through this unit is simple, and you will see it again and again: plan and practise with your AI tutor now, then carry it out with your group at your next teacher session.
bullets: You, at your own pace. You read, think and get your part ready in your own time. You can slow down on a hard idea, or move quickly through an easy one.

Your AI tutor, ready any time, day or night. Your tutor is your planning and rehearsal partner. With it you can plan roles and tasks, practise making a suggestion, rehearse sorting out a disagreement, and get friendly feedback before you meet your team.
Your teacher sessions, about twice a week. This is where the real collaboration happens. You bring the plans you prepared, and carry them out together with your group of classmates.
Your family and community. The people at home are a real team too. You can practise sharing jobs, listening and encouraging with them any day of the week.

explainers.title: Meet Nadia and her team
explainers.body:
To make each skill clear, we will follow one group of Year 5 learners all the way through the unit. They are five friends at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa: Nadia, Idil, Yusuf, Sagal and Faisal. There is no single boss among them. That is part of the point of a team: everyone matters, and everyone gets a turn to shine.

A clever team knows what each member is good at, so the jobs can be shared out well. Here is what each of them brings:

As you meet each new collaboration skill, you will see exactly what this team does with it. By the end, they will have finished a real project together. You will be doing the very same thing, with your own group, in your teacher sessions.

headers: A strength they bring to the team
rows: Organised and careful; good at planning the time and keeping the team on track.
Friendly and confident; good at talking to people and asking for help.
Practical; good at making and fixing things by hand.
Good with numbers; enjoys counting and recording answers in neat tables.
Creative; good at drawing, designing, and thinking up new ideas.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: More Books for Everyone
explainers.body:
This unit builds towards one ongoing project we call your Challenge. Collaboration only happens when people share a goal, so this Challenge belongs to a whole team.

Nadia's team noticed that many children at Ehel Academy have no books of their own at home, and the small shelf in their classroom only has a handful of tired old titles. So they chose this Challenge: how can we get more children at our school reading a book they actually enjoy? Their shared outcome became one clear sentence: more children at our school have a book they enjoy, and a comfortable place to read it.

To reach that outcome, the team has a set of jobs to share out and plan:

You do not have to copy this exact project. Any shared team goal will work: a small vegetable patch, a litter clean-up rota, a welcome pack for new students, or a shade shelter for the yard. What matters is that it is a real, shared outcome your group can reach together.
bullets: Plan a comfortable reading corner, with a shelf, cushions and a sign, in an unused part of the classroom.
Ask classmates and families for books they no longer read, to start a book swap.
Hold a small bake sale at break time to raise a little money for a few brand-new books.
Make posters and announcements to tell the whole school about the reading corner and the bake sale.
Sort the donated books onto the shelf, and keep a simple list of which books they have.
Give a short presentation to the class about the reading corner and how to use it.

explainers.title: Three stages of collaboration this year
explainers.body:
Your collaboration skills will grow in three stages this year, just as they do with research and analysis. You will begin by starting each skill, then move on to developing it, and finally you will get better at it. Here is what each stage is really about:

Do not worry if your first tries feel a little tricky. Starting is meant to feel like a first try. Each skill below will move you a little further along.
bullets: Starting — working well with your team to plan and divide our tasks, and listening to every teammate's idea before we decide.
Developing — helping the team divide tasks fairly, bringing ideas that really help, and working positively when the team hits a problem.
Getting better — planning and dividing tasks fairly by weighing everyone's skills and time, and working positively to solve a problem the team faces.

explainers.title: Skill 1: Agreeing a shared outcome
explainers.body:
Every strong team begins the same way: by agreeing on its shared outcome. A shared outcome is the one result everyone is working towards, written so clearly that every member could say it in a single sentence. Without it, five people can work hard all day and still pull in five different directions.

A good shared outcome is clear (everyone understands it the same way), shared (the whole team wants it, not just one person), and reachable (the team could really get there together). Nadia's team tested their sentence against all three before they were happy with it.

explainers.title: Skill 2: Making suggestions, and building on other people's suggestions
explainers.body:
Once a team has its shared outcome, it needs ideas. Two skills go together here. The first is making a suggestion: offering your own idea to the team. The second, and often the more useful, is building on someone else's suggestion: taking their idea and adding to it to make it even better.

Building on ideas is what turns a group of people into a team. Instead of each person pushing for their own idea, the team grows one idea together, and it usually ends up better than anything one person could have thought of alone.
bullets: I have an idea: we could ...
Even better, we could ...
Building on that, what if we also ...?
Yes, and we could add ...

explainers.title: Skill 3: Listening to others and encouraging everyone to join in
explainers.body:
A team is only as good as the voices it hears. Some people share ideas easily; others are quieter and need a warm invitation. A strong teammate does two things: they listen properly, and they encourage others to take part, especially the quieter ones.

Listening means letting a person finish, looking at them, and showing you understood, perhaps by saying their idea back to them. Encouraging means helping someone feel able to speak. When everyone is heard, the team gets more ideas, and better ones.
bullets: So you mean we could ...? (to show you listened)
You are good at this, what do you think?
We have not heard from you yet, would you like to share?
Thank you, that really helps the team.

explainers.title: Skill 4: Dividing the tasks fairly, by skill
explainers.body:
A shared outcome usually needs many jobs done. A team that shares these jobs fairly works far better than one where a single person does everything while the rest watch. The clever trick is to divide the tasks by skill: give each job to the person best suited to it, while making sure everyone has a fair share.

Dividing fairly does not mean everyone does exactly the same job. It means everyone has a reasonable share that matches their skills, so the whole team feels useful and no one is overloaded. This is one of the two ideas at the heart of collaboration this year: plan and divide tasks fairly, thinking about who is good at what and how much time everyone has.

explainers.title: Skill 5: Making a simple schedule: who, how long, and when
explainers.body:
Once the jobs are shared out, a team needs a schedule: a plan of who does each task, roughly how long it will take, and when it happens. A good schedule also thinks about which jobs can happen at the same time, called parallel tasks, and which jobs must wait for another one to finish first, called a dependency.

Here is part of the team's schedule for one session preparing the reading corner. Notice which tasks run in parallel, and which must wait:

Because tasks 2 and 3 happen in parallel, the whole plan fits into one session, even though the jobs would take longer if done one after another. That is the power of a good schedule, and it is the second half of what a strong plan needs: not just who does what, but how the timing fits together.
bullets: Parallel tasks are jobs that can be done at the same time by different people. Doing tasks in parallel means the team finishes sooner.
A dependency is a job that must wait for another job to finish first, because it needs something from it.

rows: 1. Agree where the reading corner will go
First of all; every other task depends on this.
2. Sort the donated books onto the shelf
At the same time as task 3 (parallel work).
3. Make the sign and decorate the corner
At the same time as task 2 (parallel work).
4. Write a simple list of which books they have
5. Practise what to say to invite the class in

explainers.title: Skill 6: Sorting out a disagreement in a friendly way
explainers.body:
Every team disagrees sometimes, and that is completely normal. A disagreement is not a fight, and it is not a sign of a bad team. What matters is not whether you disagree, but how you sort it out. To resolve a disagreement means to settle it fairly, so the team can move on happily.

A friendly way through a disagreement has four steps:
bullets: Listen to each side, letting each person explain their reason without being interrupted.
Find what you agree on. Almost always, both sides want the same shared outcome.
Suggest a fair middle way that takes a little from each side.
Agree and move on, without anyone feeling like the loser.

explainers.title: Skill 7: When someone is not pulling their weight
explainers.body:
Sometimes a teammate does not do their share of the work. Perhaps they forgot, perhaps the job felt too hard, or perhaps something at home got in the way. When this happens, a strong team member does not stay quiet and grumble, and does not shout either. They raise it kindly, early, before it grows into a bigger problem.

A good way to raise it is to check in gently rather than accuse: ask how the job is going, offer to help if it is stuck, and remind the person why their part matters to the shared outcome. Most of the time, a friendly check-in is all it takes. If the job is genuinely too big for one person, the team can share it out again. Working positively to solve a problem like this, instead of ignoring it or blaming someone, is exactly what a good team member does.
bullets: How is the poster going? Is there anything I can help with?
We are counting on your part for the bake sale, is everything OK?
Would it help to share that job between two of us?

explainers.title: Skill 8: Introducing useful ideas and working positively
explainers.body:
Two habits make a team a pleasure to be in. The first is introducing useful ideas: not just any idea, but one that really helps the team reach its shared outcome. The second is working positively: staying friendly and hopeful, cheering others on, and looking for what could work rather than only what could go wrong.

A useful idea usually answers a real problem the team is facing, in a way the team can actually do. Before you share an idea, it helps to ask yourself: will this really help us reach our shared outcome, and is it something our team can manage in the time we have?

explainers.title: Skill 9: Checking how your plan is going
explainers.body:
A plan is only useful if the team keeps checking it. Every so often, a good team stops for a moment and asks: which parts are finished, which parts have we started, and which parts have we not touched yet? This is called checking a plan, and it helps a team notice a problem early, while there is still time to fix it.

A simple way to check is to mark each task as Not started, Started, or Done, and talk together about anything still Not started close to the deadline. Checking is not about worrying or rushing. It is a calm habit that keeps a team's promise to itself.
bullets: Not started — the task has not begun yet.
Started — the task is under way, but not finished.
Done — the task is complete.

explainers.title: How collaboration helps the other five skills
explainers.body:
Collaboration does not work on its own. It makes every other Global Perspectives skill stronger, and they make it stronger too.

So the teamwork you practise now will lift all your other skills. Learning to collaborate well is one of the most useful things you will do this year.
bullets: Research gets easier, because a team can share out the finding-out and gather far more than one person could.
Analysis grows, because teammates notice different causes and reasons that you might miss alone.
Evaluation improves, because a team can weigh an idea from many sides before deciding.
Reflection deepens, because you learn about yourself by noticing how you work with others.
Communication matters more than ever, because a team only works if its members share their ideas clearly.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: the collaboration cycle
explainers.body: You have now met every collaboration skill in this unit. Here is how they fit together into one cycle you can use for any team project:
bullets: Agree a clear shared outcome the whole team wants.
Share ideas, making suggestions and building on each other's.
Listen to everyone and encourage the quieter voices.
Divide the tasks fairly, by each person's skill.
Make a simple schedule: who, how long, and when, using parallel work and dependencies.
Sort out any disagreements in a friendly way.
Notice kindly if someone is not pulling their weight, and offer to help.
Introduce useful ideas, and keep working positively.
Check how the plan is going, and fix anything that has stalled.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Communication. Once you can work well in a team, communication teaches you to share your ideas and findings clearly, so that others truly understand you. Good collaboration and good communication go hand in hand: a team needs both. Well done for learning to be someone people are glad to have on their team.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: In Global Perspectives, the topic is like a boat, and the skill is where the boat takes you.
In this unit the topic is a real project: a reading corner, a book swap, and a bake sale.
But the real prize is not the reading corner. It is to become someone people are glad to have on their team.

bigIdeas.title: Two questions every team keeps asking
lines: How well do I work with my team? Do I make useful suggestions, encourage others, and help solve problems?
How well do we work as a team? Do we make a plan, divide the work fairly, and check how it is going?
Coming back to these two questions is one of the best ways to become a stronger teammate.

bigIdeas.title: Four steps to sort out a disagreement
lines: Listen to each side without interrupting.
Find what both sides agree on, usually the same shared outcome.
Suggest a fair middle way that takes a little from each side.
Agree and move on, so no one feels like the loser.

bigIdeas.title: If a teammate is not pulling their weight
lines: Check in kindly and early, before it becomes a bigger problem.
Ask how the job is going, and offer to help if it is stuck.
Remind them why their part matters to the shared outcome.
If the job is genuinely too big, share it out again rather than letting it sit undone.

lines: Say hello to your AI tutor and tell it: I am starting Unit 5 of Global Perspectives, and the skill is Collaboration.
Ask it: in one or two simple sentences, why is being a good teammate useful, even outside of school?
Then tell your tutor about a time you worked well in a team, and a time teamwork was hard, and why.

lines: Tell your AI tutor about a team project you could do, real or imagined.
Ask it to help you write your shared outcome as one clear sentence, starting with the words Our shared outcome is.
Then ask: is my shared outcome clear, shared, and something a team could really reach?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor

Ask it to check your sentence against all three tests: is it clear, is it shared, and is it reachable?
Ask the tutor to help you make the sentence sharper and simpler if it needs it.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one suggestion for your team project, starting with We could.
Ask the tutor to build on your idea, then you build on its idea, back and forth, three times.
Notice how the idea grows. Ask the tutor which version of the idea is strongest, and why.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor

Ask it to give you three friendly sentences you could use to encourage a quiet teammate to speak.
Then practise: the tutor plays a quiet team member, and you gently invite its idea.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your list of tasks and who is doing each one.
Ask it to help you sort them into a schedule with who, how long, and when.
Then ask: which of my tasks could be done in parallel, and which ones depend on another task being finished first?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor

Ask the tutor to take the other side, then practise the four steps: listen, find what you agree on, suggest a middle way, agree.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor

Ask it: which step do I find easiest, and which do I find hardest, and why?
Ask the tutor to suggest one step to focus on with your real team next.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor

Ask it: is my shared outcome clear, and is it something a team of children could really reach?
Ask the tutor to help you make the sentence sharper and simpler.

Ask the tutor which version of the idea is strongest, and why.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor

toolkit.title: The collaboration cycle at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever your team project, good collaboration follows the same steps. Come back to this list whenever you feel lost.
items: Agree a shared outcome: the one result the whole team wants.
Share ideas: make suggestions and build on each other's.
Listen and encourage: hear everyone, especially the quiet voices.
Divide the tasks: fairly, and by each person's skill.
Schedule: who does what, how long, and when, using parallel work and dependencies.
Sort out disagreements: fairly and in a friendly way.
Notice kindly if someone is not pulling their weight, and offer to help.
Introduce useful ideas, and keep working positively.
Check how the plan is going, and fix anything that has stalled.

toolkit.title: The Collaboration skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Collaboration means working together with other people to reach a shared goal, called a shared outcome. It is not just being in the same room. A team is collaborating when they share one outcome, share out the work fairly, and help each other get there.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, plan and divide tasks fairly, thinking about who is good at what and how much time you have. Second, bring ideas that will really help, and work positively to solve the problems your team faces. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

toolkit.title: Your Stage 5 Collaboration learning goals
toolkit.intro: Your collaboration skills grow in three stages this year. Here are the real learning goals for each stage, in simple words. Your teacher may talk about these.

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for making and building on suggestions
toolkit.intro: Use these to add your own ideas, and to grow other people's ideas instead of blocking them.
items: I have an idea: we could ...
What if we tried ...?
Even better, we could ...
Building on that, what if we also ...?
Yes, and we could add ...
That gives me an idea: what about ...?

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for listening and encouraging others
toolkit.intro: Use these to make sure everyone is heard, especially the quieter members of your team.
items: So you mean we could ...? (to show you listened)
That is a good start, tell us more.
You are good at this, what do you think?
We have not heard from you yet, would you like to share?
I like that idea because ...
Thank you, that really helps the team.

toolkit.title: Dividing tasks fairly, by skill
toolkit.intro: Share the jobs so that each one matches a person's skill, and everyone has a fair share. Copy this table to plan the division.

toolkit.title: A schedule grid: who, how long, when
toolkit.intro: Turn your tasks into a schedule. In the last column, show the order and the links: write First, or After task 2, or At the same time as task 3. Remember, parallel tasks happen together, and a dependency must wait for another task to finish.

toolkit.title: Sorting out a disagreement: a step-by-step guide
toolkit.intro:
Disagreements are normal. What matters is how you sort them out. Follow these four steps.

Keep your voice calm and friendly. Deal with the problem, never the person. A disagreement resolved well often makes a team stronger than before.
items: Listen to each side, letting each person explain without being interrupted.
Find what you agree on, which is almost always the same shared outcome.
Suggest a fair middle way that takes a little from each side.
Agree and move on, so no one feels like the loser.

toolkit.title: If someone is not pulling their weight
toolkit.intro: This happens to every team sometimes. Raise it kindly and early, using steps like these, rather than staying quiet or getting cross.
items: Check in gently: ask how the job is going, rather than accusing.
Offer to help if the job feels stuck or too big.
Remind them why their part matters to the shared outcome.
If it is genuinely too much for one person, share the job out again.

toolkit.title: Checking how your plan is going
toolkit.intro: Stop every so often and mark each task honestly. A Not started task close to the deadline is not a failure; it just shows the team where to put its energy next.

toolkit.title: A good team member and a good team
toolkit.intro: Use these as a checklist for how to behave in a team.

toolkit.title: A good team member ...
items: always listens, does their fair share, and encourages others.
always shares ideas and builds on other people's.
never puts a teammate down or takes over every job.
raises a problem kindly instead of staying quiet or getting cross.

toolkit.title: A good team ...
items: always agrees a shared outcome and divides the work fairly.
always checks its plan and helps a teammate who is stuck.
never leaves one person to do everything, or ignores a quiet voice.

toolkit.title: Making the most of your teacher sessions
toolkit.intro: Remember the pattern of this unit: plan and practise with your AI tutor, then do the real teamwork with your group in your teacher sessions. Here is how to make each session count.
items: Come prepared: bring the plan or schedule you drafted with your AI tutor.
Start by agreeing your shared outcome, and what you want to finish in this session.
Share out the jobs quickly, using each person's skill, so no time is wasted.
Listen to everyone, and check the quieter members have had their say.
Near the end, check the plan together and agree who does what before next time.

checklists.title: Ready for your next teacher session
checklists.intro: Bring these things to your teacher session, so your real teamwork can start straight away.
items: Your shared outcome, written as one clear sentence.
Your list of tasks, with an idea of who could do each one.
Your schedule, showing who, how long, and when.
Anything you drafted with your AI tutor that your group needs to agree on together.
Any question you were not sure about, to ask your teacher or your group.

challenge.intro:
You have now planned a real team project. Pull it together by completing these three sentences about your teamwork, in your own words:

Keep this checkpoint safe. You will look back at it during Reflection, and it will show you how much your collaboration has grown.
checkpoints: One thing we found hard was ...

activities.title: Choose your project and your shared outcome
activities.label: Activity 1: Choose your project and your shared outcome
activities.intro: Every team starts by agreeing what it is working towards. First choose a project, then write your shared outcome: the one result the whole team wants, in a single clear sentence. A good shared outcome is small enough for your team to reach, but big enough to be worth doing. If you are not sure, start with one of the ideas above and make it your own.
steps: Write the project you will work on: 'Our team project is ...'.
Write your shared outcome in one sentence: 'Our shared outcome is ...'.
Write one reason this matters, both to your team and to your school or community.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your project and your shared outcome sentence.
Ask it: is my shared outcome clear, and is it something a team of children could really reach?
Ask the tutor to help you make the sentence sharper and simpler.

activities.title: Make a suggestion, then build on others
activities.label: Activity 2: Make a suggestion, then build on others
activities.intro: Great teams grow one idea together instead of fighting for separate ones. Here you practise making a suggestion and building on other people's ideas. Building on an idea is almost always better than blocking it.
steps: Write one suggestion for your project, starting with 'We could ...'.
Now build on it twice, as if you were a teammate: 'Even better, we could ...' and 'Building on that, what if we ...'.
Notice how the idea gets stronger each time you add to it.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your first suggestion.
Take turns building on it: the tutor adds an idea, then you add to the tutor's idea, three times in all.
Ask the tutor which version of the idea is strongest, and why.

activities.title: Listen and encourage everyone to join in
activities.label: Activity 3: Listen and encourage everyone to join in
activities.intro: A strong teammate makes sure quieter voices are heard too. Practise a friendly way to invite someone into a conversation, and a way to show you were really listening.
steps: Write one sentence you could say to show a teammate you listened to their idea.
Write one sentence you could say to encourage a quiet teammate to share.
Think of a time you felt too shy to speak up. What would have helped you join in?

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about a quiet teammate, real or imagined, who has not shared an idea yet.
Ask it to help you write a kind way to invite them in.
Practise saying it out loud, with the tutor playing the quiet teammate.

activities.title: Divide the tasks fairly, by skill
activities.label: Activity 4: Divide the tasks fairly, by skill
activities.intro: Now share the jobs your project needs so that each one matches a person's skill, and everyone has a fair share.
steps: List at least five tasks your project needs done.
Next to each task, write the skill it needs, and who could do it, and why.
Check together: does anyone have too much to do, or too little?

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your list of tasks and skills to your AI tutor.
Ask it: does my way of sharing the jobs look fair, or does anyone have too much?
Ask the tutor if any task needs a skill I have not planned for.

activities.title: Make a simple schedule
activities.label: Activity 5: Make a simple schedule
activities.intro: Turn your task list into a schedule. Show who does each task, roughly how long it will take, and when it happens, including which tasks can run in parallel and which have a dependency.
steps: List your tasks in the order they need to happen.
For each one, write who does it, how long it should take, and when.
Mark any tasks that could run in parallel, and any that must wait for another task first.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your schedule to your AI tutor.
Ask it: which of my tasks could be done in parallel, to save time?
Ask the tutor which task must be done first, because other tasks depend on it.

activities.title: Sort out a disagreement in a friendly way
activities.label: Activity 6: Sort out a disagreement in a friendly way
activities.intro: Think of a disagreement your team might have about your project, such as which games to sell at the bake sale, or where exactly the reading corner should go. Practise the four steps to sort it out.
steps: Write the two sides of a possible disagreement, fairly, as if you agreed with both.
Write what both sides agree on underneath.
Write a fair middle way that takes a little from each side.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe the disagreement to your AI tutor, and ask it to take the other side.
Practise the four steps out loud, all the way to agreeing a middle way.
Ask the tutor for feedback: did I listen, stay calm, and treat the other side fairly?

activities.title: When someone is not pulling their weight
activities.label: Activity 7: When someone is not pulling their weight
activities.intro: Every team meets this sometimes. Plan a kind, early way to raise it, rather than staying quiet or getting cross.
steps: Imagine a teammate has not finished their part, and the deadline is close. Write what you notice.
Write a kind check-in sentence you could say to them.
Write one way the job could be shared out again, if it really is too much for one person.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about the teammate in your scenario who is not pulling their weight.
Ask it to help you plan a kind check-in, and one way to share the job again if it is needed.
Ask the tutor for feedback: does my plan sound kind, or does it sound like blaming?

activities.title: Introduce a useful idea and work positively
activities.label: Activity 8: Introduce a useful idea and work positively
activities.intro: Think of a real problem your team project faces, and practise introducing one useful idea to help solve it, in a positive way.
steps: Write the problem your team is facing.
Write one idea that would really help, and check it against your shared outcome.
Write one positive sentence you could say to keep the team's spirits up while solving it.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one problem your team is facing.
Ask it to help you think of a useful idea, and check it against the shared outcome.
Ask the tutor for one way to say a difficult thing to a teammate positively, without a put-down.

activities.title: Check how your plan is going
activities.label: Activity 9: Check how your plan is going
activities.intro: Stop and check your schedule honestly. Mark each task as Not started, Started, or Done, and decide together what to do about anything still Not started.
steps: Copy your task list, and mark each one Not started, Started, or Done.
Write one task that needs attention soonest, and why.
Write one calm change your team could make to keep the plan on track.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your task list to your AI tutor, with a status for each: Not started, Started, or Done.
Ask it: if one task is still Not started near the deadline, what should our team do?
Ask the tutor for one tip to help a team check its plan calmly, without panicking.

activities.title: Your team checkpoint
activities.label: Your team checkpoint
activities.intro:
You have now planned a real team project. Pull it together by finishing these three sentences about your teamwork, in your own words:

Keep this checkpoint safe. You will look back at it during Reflection, and it will show you how much your collaboration has grown.
steps: Our team worked best when ...
One thing we found hard was ...
Next time, our team will ...

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three team sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it: from what I said, what is one thing I could do to be an even better teammate?
Ask the tutor to help you plan your very next step with your group.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 12 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Give your own words rather than copying from the other files.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does collaboration mean?
practice.answer: Collaboration means working together with other people to reach a shared goal. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: The one result a whole team is working towards is called the shared ______.
practice.answer: Outcome (the shared outcome).

practice.prompt: True or false: a team is any group of children sitting in the same room.
practice.answer: False. A team is collaborating only when they share one outcome, share the work, and help each other.

practice.prompt: When a teammate makes a suggestion and you add to it to make it better, you are ______ on their suggestion.
practice.answer: Building (building on their suggestion).

practice.prompt: Name one thing you could say to encourage a quieter teammate to share their idea.
practice.answer: Any friendly invitation, such as: You are good at this, what do you think? or We have not heard from you yet, would you like to share?

practice.prompt: When you share out the jobs, you should divide them ______ and by each person's ______.
practice.answer: Fairly; skill (divide the tasks fairly, by each person's skill).

practice.prompt: In a schedule, two tasks that can be done at the same time are called ______ tasks.
practice.answer: Parallel tasks.

practice.prompt: A task that cannot start until another task is finished has a ______ on that task.
practice.answer: A dependency (it depends on the other task being finished first).

practice.prompt: When two teammates disagree, name one good thing to do first.
practice.answer: Listen to each side without interrupting. (Also correct: find what both sides agree on.)

practice.prompt: If a teammate is not pulling their weight, what should you do first?
practice.answer: Check in kindly and early, asking how the job is going, rather than staying quiet or accusing them.

practice.prompt: Name one thing a useful idea should do for your team.
practice.answer: It should really help the team reach its shared outcome, and be something the team can actually manage.

practice.prompt: Name the three statuses a team can use to check how a task is going.
practice.answer: Not started, Started, and Done.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each collaboration word (1 to 6) to the correct meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Shared outcome
options: A. To share the tasks out between the team members.
B. The one result the whole team is working towards.
C. A job that must wait until another job is finished first.
D. The part you add to help your team, such as an idea or a job.
E. To sort out a disagreement fairly, so the team can move on.
F. Jobs that can be done at the same time by different people.
practice.answer: B — The one result the whole team is working towards.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Contribution
practice.answer: D — The part you add to help your team, such as an idea or a job.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Divide
practice.answer: A — To share the tasks out between the team members.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Resolve
practice.answer: E — To sort out a disagreement fairly, so the team can move on.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Dependency
practice.answer: C — A job that must wait until another job is finished first.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Parallel tasks
practice.answer: F — Jobs that can be done at the same time by different people.

practice.intro: These short scenarios ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Faisal has a good idea but is too shy to say it, and the group is talking quickly. What could Idil do to help?
practice.answer: Idil could listen for a pause and gently invite Faisal in, for example by saying: Faisal, you are good at ideas, what do you think? This encourages the quieter voice.

practice.prompt: Two teammates both want the fun job of decorating the reading corner, and neither wants to count the donated books. How could the team divide the work fairly?
practice.answer: They could divide by skill and take turns, so the enjoyable jobs and the less exciting jobs are shared out, and each person does something that suits them.

practice.prompt: The team cannot make the sign until they know exactly where the reading corner will go. What is this link called, and which task should be scheduled first?
practice.answer: This link is a dependency. Deciding where the corner will go should be scheduled first, because the sign depends on it.

practice.prompt: Yusuf was meant to bring the shelf for the reading corner, but two sessions have passed and it still has not arrived. What should the team do?
practice.answer: The team should check in with Yusuf kindly, ask if something is making the job hard, offer to help, and if needed, share the job out so the shelf still gets done in time.

reflection.prompt: Working on my own, at my own pace ...
Planning and practising with my AI tutor before I met my team ...
Doing the real teamwork with my group in our teacher sessions ...
Practising teamwork with my family or neighbours ...
Seeing our shared project come together, after all our planning ...

selfAssessment.statement: I can work well with my team to plan our tasks.
I can agree a clear shared outcome with my team.
I can make a suggestion and build on other people's ideas.
I can listen to others and encourage everyone to join in.
I can help divide the tasks fairly, by each person's skill.
I can help make a simple schedule for my team.
I can help sort out a disagreement in a friendly way.
I can say something kind and helpful if a teammate is not pulling their weight.
I can introduce a useful idea and work positively.
I can check how my team's plan is going, and help fix it if needed.

vocabulary.meaning: Working together with other people to reach a shared goal.
The one result the whole team is working towards.
The part you add to help your team, such as an idea or a job.
To share the tasks out between the team members.
In a way that gives everyone a reasonable share.
The things a person is good at, such as drawing, planning or building.
A plan of who does each task, how long it will take, and when.
Jobs that can be done at the same time by different people.
A task that must wait until another task is finished first.
A time when team members do not agree; a normal part of teamwork.
To sort out a disagreement fairly, so the team can move on.
To help someone feel able to join in and share their ideas.
An idea you offer to help your team.
To take someone's idea and add to it, making it even better.
In a friendly, hopeful way, even when something is hard.
People working together, each doing their part, to reach a shared goal.
A job that needs to be done.
To decide, before you start, what your team will do and how.
A moment when a team stops to see how its plan is going.
Doing a fair share of the team's work.

mistakes: Starting the work before agreeing a clear shared outcome.
One person doing every job while the others watch.
Blocking a teammate's idea instead of building on it.
Forgetting the quieter members, so their good ideas are never heard.
Letting a disagreement turn into an argument instead of resolving it kindly.
Making a plan but never checking how it is going.
Saying nothing when a teammate is not pulling their weight, until the whole team is frustrated.
